docs.title: Connect a user’s account
docs.content:
# Connect a user’s account

## When to connect an account

Use this flow when your application needs another person's private portfolios. For public market data, use your ordinary API key and `bharosa.markets`; do not ask users to connect an account. For your own private data, enable the appropriate own-account permissions on your key.

## Before you begin

Register your application in Bharosa Developer settings, add its exact HTTPS return URL, wait for sign-in setup to be ready, and create its backend credential. This is a delegated application credential, not a personal API key. Keep it on your server. Your user must already have a session in your application; bind the connection attempt to that session.

The connection transport uses the console origin, `https://app.bharosa.finance`, while SDK resource calls use `https://api.bharosa.finance`. Do not substitute `/auth/login` or `/auth/callback` for these operations, or call Bharosa's internal approval handlers yourself. Redirect the user to the authorization URL returned by session creation.

## 1. Start a connection on your server

Protect your own start endpoint with your application's session, same-origin check and CSRF protection. Generate independent 32-byte random values encoded as unpadded base64url for `state`, the receipt verifier and the server-session secret. Persist them in your encrypted durable store before making the request. Retain a stable creation idempotency key so a lost response does not start a second connection. An Idempotency-Key must be 16–128 printable non-space ASCII characters; a saved crypto.randomUUID() value fits this requirement.

Send `POST /connect/v1/sessions` with `Authorization: Bearer <backend credential>`, `X-Bharosa-Server-Session: <secret>`, `Idempotency-Key: <stable operation ID>` and `Content-Type: application/json`.

The return URL is illustrative: use the exact URL registered for your application. The scope list is nonempty and has no duplicates. Request only what the app needs and what its registration and backend credential permit. This request does not choose an account ID: the authenticated consenting user determines the account. Portfolio selection inside your UI is a display filter, not a narrower provider grant.

A `201` response contains `id`, `authorization_url`, `approval_expires_at` and `session_expires_at`. The dates are Unix seconds. Save the ID with the pending attempt, validate the returned authorization URL against the expected HTTPS Bharosa origin, then redirect that same user to it. Never send the server-session secret or backend credential to the browser.

## 2. Validate the return before exchanging anything

Bharosa returns to your registered URL with `bharosa_request`, `bharosa_state`, and either `bharosa_code` or `bharosa_error`. Supported errors here are `access_denied` and `expired`. Reject duplicate security parameters, unsolicited callbacks, expired attempts, a missing/mismatched initiating session, incorrect state and a mixture of code and error. The receipt code is not an API access token.

For denial or expiry, clear the pending UI state and offer a new connection; do not exchange a code or mark the user connected. For approval, use a stable exchange operation ID bound to the saved attempt. Exchange the same receipt with the same ID after a lost response; do not create a different exchange operation for an already consumed receipt. Serialize callback handling in the durable store to avoid concurrent refresh or exchange races.

Send `POST /connect/v1/sessions/{id}/exchange` with the same application credential and server-session secret, an `Idempotency-Key`, and JSON `{ "code": "<returned receipt>", "code_verifier": "<saved verifier>" }`. A `200` response contains `grant_id`, `generation`, `account_id`, `scopes`, `delivery_id`, and `status: "delivery_pending"`. The account and granted scopes come from this server response, not browser form data.

## 3. Receive and save the access token

Send `POST /connect/v1/sessions/{id}/deliveries/{delivery_id}/retrieve` with the application credential, server-session secret and JSON `{}`. Its `200` response contains `delivery_id`, `grant_id`, `generation`, `account_id`, `scopes`, `access_token`, `token_type: "Bearer"`, and `expires_at` (Unix seconds).

Validate the response and atomically save the token with its grant, account, scopes, generation and expiry in your encrypted server store. Save before acknowledging. Then send `POST /connect/v1/sessions/{id}/deliveries/{delivery_id}/ack` with JSON `{}`; success is `204` with no body. An acknowledged or expired delivery cannot be retrieved again (`410 delivery_unavailable`). Never log these responses or return tokens to browser JavaScript.

Create one immutable SDK client per grant. Check the granted scopes before offering a feature, and paginate lists. Keep the browser on your own authenticated backend endpoints; it should receive only the portfolio data needed for the screen.

## 4. Recover pending delivery and refresh

`GET /connect/v1/sessions/{id}` returns session status and expiry. Once redeemed, it also returns grant/delivery metadata. It never returns a token. Respect polling limits: at least two seconds between polls per session, and no more than 60 polls per minute across the application. A `429` response supplies `Retry-After: 2`; wait at least two seconds before retrying. A retry delay does not guarantee that processing has finished.

To refresh, send `POST /connect/v1/sessions/{id}/grants/{grant_id}/refresh` with JSON `{}` and a stable `Idempotency-Key`. A `202` response identifies the grant and delivery, with delivery state. Retrieve, persist and acknowledge the replacement delivery as above, then construct a new SDK client. There is no provider refresh token for your app to manage. Serialize refresh per grant. A pending earlier delivery must be recovered first; `409 reconnect_required` requires a fresh connection, not an unbounded retry.

Session expiry prevents these control and delivery operations; it is not a promise that an already issued access token has been revoked. Use the returned expiry fields, not a hardcoded session lifetime. Receipt redemption is short-lived, so process the return promptly.

## 5. Disconnect explicitly

Protect your own disconnect endpoint with session, Origin and CSRF checks. Send `POST /connect/v1/sessions/{id}/grants/{grant_id}/disconnect` with JSON `{}`. Success is `200` with `grant_id`, `revoked: true`, and `provider_revocation`. Bharosa resource access is fenced locally; pending provider cleanup is not proof that every upstream token family has been removed. Preserve the returned cleanup state without exposing credentials.

Remove the local token and stop background reads. If the network response is lost, do not tell the user revocation succeeded: retain the necessary encrypted control record for recovery while blocking further local reads. `DELETE /connect/v1/sessions/{id}` returns `204`, revokes its attached local grant, ends the session and queues upstream cleanup. It does not certify completed provider revocation.

## Common errors

All server-to-server connection calls require both the backend credential and server-session header. Do not send browser cookies, an Origin header, a user-token header, `X-API-Key`, or query parameters to `/connect/v1/` endpoints. JSON bodies use `application/json`; empty POST bodies are `{}`, not an absent body. Redirect following must be disabled when sending secrets.

Errors have `error.type`, `error.code`, `error.message`, `error.param` and `error.request_id`, plus a `Request-Id` response header. Record the request ID and status without secret headers, callback URLs or token bodies. Distinguish malformed input (`400`), failed credentials (`401`), unavailable foreign resources (`404`), conflicting/reconnect states (`409`), expired delivery (`410`), media type (`415`), rate limiting (`429`) and temporary service failures (`503`). Do not turn all errors into a new consent attempt.

The examples describe implemented transport behavior. They do not certify a new hosted end-to-end connection or broaden application permissions.

## Server request helpers

Save these JavaScript helpers as connection-requests.mjs in your server project. They use Node’s built-in fetch and crypto; no private Bharosa imports are needed. Pass your backend credential and the saved server-session secret. These functions intentionally do not provide your session database or a production web server. Implement the durable storage, authenticated session, response validation and CSRF checks described above before connecting real users.

A failed request exposes status, a sanitized code and requestId without returning the raw token-bearing body. Reuse saved operation IDs after response loss. Validate every successful response before trusting its IDs, scopes, expiry or token; the helper performs transport only.

docs.title: Retrieve scheme performance
docs.content:
# Retrieve scheme performance

## What this measures

Scheme performance measures changes in a scheme's NAV. It is not an investor's return: it does not incorporate the investor's purchases, withdrawals or cash-flow timing. Choose the exact Direct or Regular plan and Growth option before comparing results. IDCW distributions are not reconstructed into a return.

Use a server-side `Bharosa` client configured with an API key. Enable the optional own-account `accounts:read` permission, which these methods require. Follow Your own account to create the key and configure the client once. These methods are account-scoped: baseline `bharosa.markets` access alone does not include them. No portfolio write permission is needed.

Choose a first-of-month `asOf` date, such as 2026-10-01. This is the requested cutoff, not a claim that a price was observed on that day. Each result exposes the actual observations used. Monthly access does not require separate market-data approval.

## Request a dated return

GET /v1/accounts/{account}/market-data/schemes/{id}/performance. account is your authorized account context; id is the positive numeric scheme ID returned by scheme search. Pass the user's selected match, rather than assuming the first search result is the intended plan.

The SDK requires `asOf`. Optional `periods` accepts 1y, 3y, 5y and `since_inception`; when omitted, the API requests 1y, 3y and 5y. HTTP uses `as_of` and comma-separated `periods`. Inception results require verified scheme inception evidence; the first row available in a partial dataset is not sufficient.

## Call the API directly

Set BHAROSA_SECRET_KEY on your server with accounts:read enabled for your own account (required for these methods). Set SELECTED_SCHEME_ID or SELECTED_CATEGORY to the identifier your application selected. These account-scoped analytics requests are not included in baseline market access; never put a secret key in browser code.

## Read the result

Every response includes `requested_as_of` (the requested YYYY-MM-DD cutoff), `currency` (INR), `methodology_version` (the calculation definition), `source_cutoff` (the source cutoff date), `source_version` (source revision identifier) and `warnings` (an array of messages to retain when presenting the result). Source metadata is not a promise of today's prices.

Each metric is an `object` with `status`, `value` and `reason`. When `status` is available, `value` is a decimal string and `reason` is null. When `status` is unavailable, `value` is null and `reason` explains the missing result. These fields are present even when the `value` is null; null is not zero. Percentage strings such as 10 represent ten percent, not 0.10. Preserve the string until you deliberately format it for display.

`freshness_policy` reports `nav_days`, `category_min_funds` and `category_min_coverage_pct`, so callers can see the limits applied. Its `aum_days` and `ter_days` fields are shared metadata, not evidence that AUM or TER comparison endpoints are available.

`object` is `scheme_performance`. `scheme_id` and `fund_id` identify the scheme and its parent mutual fund; `plan`, `option` and `basis` describe the selection and valuation basis. `available_history_start`, `scheme_nav_inception_date` and `inception_basis` are nullable: missing or unverified evidence remains explicit. A verified `inception_basis` is `verified_first_scheme_nav`.

`periods` is an array. Each entry identifies `period`, `requested_start` (nullable for unresolved inception) and `requested_end`, with its own `status` and nullable `reason`. `total_return_pct` and `cagr_pct` are separate metric objects: a total return may be available while CAGR is unavailable. CAGR is only available when the observed interval is more than 365 days.

`start_observation_date` and `end_observation_date` are the actual YYYY-MM-DD NAV dates. `start_nav` and `end_nav` are nullable decimal-string prices per unit. `start_lag_days` and `end_lag_days` are nullable calendar-day distances from the requested boundaries; `elapsed_days` is the nullable distance between actual observations. Inspect them rather than assuming the requested date had a price.

`annualization_basis` is `observed_nav_dates_365_25`: CAGR uses elapsed observed days divided by 365.25. `calculation_precision` is `decimal_inputs_float64_returns`; Total return uses exact rational arithmetic on decimal NAV inputs; CAGR uses floating-point exponentiation. Output percentage precision is bounded to eight decimal places. The result is not a guarantee of future performance.

## Handle missing data and errors

For 401, check whether the account key is expired or revoked. For 403, check that the `accounts:read` permission is enabled and the monthly date is valid; baseline market access alone does not authorize account analytics. A 400 means the inputs need correction, such as an unsupported period or metric. A 404 means the selected resource is absent or unavailable in this context; confirm the identifier from the resource selection step. On 503, report temporary market-data unavailability and offer a retry rather than showing zero.

A successful HTTP 200 can contain unavailable `metrics`. Check each metric's `status` before rendering its `value` and keep its `reason` visible. Do not turn a missing return into a ranking or an investment recommendation.

docs.content:
# Retrieve category returns

## What a category average means

A category groups mutual funds by classification. The return statistic averages eligible funds with equal weights after deduplicating funds; it is not an investable index or the return on a portfolio you own. Current classification is applied to historical prices, so survivorship and reclassification can affect comparisons.

Use a server-side `Bharosa` client configured with an API key. Enable the optional own-account `accounts:read` permission, which these methods require. Follow Your own account to create the key and configure the client once. These methods are account-scoped: baseline `bharosa.markets` access alone does not include them. No portfolio write permission is needed.

Choose a first-of-month `asOf` date, such as 2026-10-01. This is the requested cutoff, not a claim that a price was observed on that day. Each result exposes the actual observations used. Monthly access does not require separate market-data approval.

## Choose the category and plan

GET /v1/accounts/{account}/market-data/categories/{`category`}/statistics. `category` is the exact classification identifier, not a numeric fund ID or a display label. Use an identifier confirmed by your `category` data source; index_fund is a verified identifier. A generic label such as equity is not a universal `category` ID.

`asOf` is required. `periods` accepts 1y, 3y and 5y, defaulting to all three; `since_inception` is unsupported for categories. `metrics` accepts only return and defaults to it. `plan` is direct or regular (default direct); `option` is growth. HTTP parameters are `as_of`, comma-separated `periods` and `metrics`, `plan` and `option`. AUM, TER and investor-return statistics are not offered by this `method`.

## Call the API directly

Set BHAROSA_SECRET_KEY on your server with accounts:read enabled for your own account (required for these methods). Set SELECTED_SCHEME_ID or SELECTED_CATEGORY to the identifier your application selected. These account-scoped analytics requests are not included in baseline market access; never put a secret key in browser code.

## Inspect coverage before comparing

Every response includes `requested_as_of` (the requested YYYY-MM-DD cutoff), `currency` (INR), `methodology_version` (the calculation definition), `source_cutoff` (the source cutoff date), `source_version` (source revision identifier) and `warnings` (an array of messages to retain when presenting the result). Source metadata is not a promise of today's prices.

Each metric is an `object` with `status`, `value` and `reason`. When `status` is available, `value` is a decimal string and `reason` is null. When `status` is unavailable, `value` is null and `reason` explains the missing result. These fields are present even when the `value` is null; null is not zero. Percentage strings such as 10 represent ten percent, not 0.10. Preserve the string until you deliberately format it for display.

`freshness_policy` reports `nav_days`, `category_min_funds` and `category_min_coverage_pct`, so callers can see the limits applied. Its `aum_days` and `ter_days` fields are shared metadata, not evidence that AUM or TER comparison endpoints are available.

`object` is `category_statistics` and `category` echoes the identifier. `cohort` contains `policy` (`current_classification_as_of_prices`), `plan`, `option`, `fund_count`, `selected_scheme_count` and nullable `classification_date`. Counts describe this selected `cohort`; they are not the size of the entire market.

`metrics` maps metric names to result objects. Each includes the `status`/`value`/`reason` fields described above, `method` (`equal_weighted_arithmetic_mean`), nullable `return_type` (total_return or cagr) and `unit`. Inspect the returned `return_type` instead of treating total and annualized returns as interchangeable.

`eligible_count` is the `cohort` eligible for consideration; `valid_count` is the number usable for the statistic. `missing_count`, `stale_count` and `invalid_count` explain excluded observations, and `exclusions` maps `reason` codes to counts. `coverage_pct` is a decimal-string percentage. At least three valid funds and 80% coverage are required; otherwise the metric is unavailable.

`observation_date_min` and `observation_date_max` are nullable bounds on actual observation dates. `observed_elapsed_days_min` and `observed_elapsed_days_max` report nullable observed durations. `start_lag_days_max` and `end_lag_days_max` report the largest nullable boundary lag. These fields let you see when underlying observations differ across funds; the requested cutoff alone cannot establish comparability.

## Handle unavailable categories

For 401, check whether the account key is expired or revoked. For 403, check that the `accounts:read` permission is enabled and the monthly date is valid; baseline market access alone does not authorize account analytics. A 400 means the inputs need correction, such as an unsupported period or metric. A 404 means the selected resource is absent or unavailable in this context; confirm the identifier from the resource selection step. On 503, report temporary market-data unavailability and offer a retry rather than showing zero.

A successful HTTP 200 can contain unavailable `metrics`. Check each metric's `status` before rendering its `value` and keep its `reason` visible. Do not turn a missing return into a ranking or an investment recommendation.

docs.content:
# The mutual fund object

## What a mutual fund represents

A mutual fund owns a disclosed portfolio of underlying investments. An investible scheme identifies the plan and option a person holds; its NAV and expense observations belong to that scheme. The AMC is the organization managing funds, not the fund or scheme itself.

A fund’s disclosed portfolio is different from an investor’s portfolio. The first describes what the fund invests in; the second describes what a person owns. Do not interchange their identifiers.

## Object contract under review

Documentation proposal for review. This page describes the intended public resource organization, not a newly available endpoint. HTTP routes, SDK signatures and additional response fields still need agreement; no request is shown as executable.

The existing account-scoped fund-portfolio response includes a fund owner ID and disclosure data. That does not establish a standalone public fund catalogue or retrieve operation. The intended fund object needs a stable identity and explicit links to its disclosed portfolios and related schemes; exact fields and discovery guarantees remain undecided.

Do not derive a fund ID from a scheme ID, AMC ID or a fictional example. Until a public discovery interface is agreed, existing fund snapshot calls require an owner ID resolved through the supported mapping in the integration environment.

docs.content:
# The scheme object

## Choose an exact scheme

An investor selects a scheme, including its plan and option. Similar names do not make two schemes interchangeable. The current search response supplies a `scheme_id` for market snapshots and an `instrument.id` for investor portfolio positions. Use the identifier required by the particular operation.

NAV is a price per unit for the scheme. Expense ratios are observations associated with that scheme. Fund portfolios and underlying holdings belong to the fund owner; they are not investor positions or separate scheme-owned portfolios.

This object page organizes existing concepts. A unified standalone public scheme-object response, list and retrieve interface remain proposals. Existing search/reference and monthly snapshot response fields retain their implemented meaning.

docs.title: Holdings, snapshots and history
docs.content:
# Holdings, snapshots and history

## Snapshots preserve what was reported

The manual snapshot API saves a complete set of entered positions and their effective date. A replacement creates a new snapshot and makes it current; it leaves the previous snapshot unchanged. Omitted positions are removed from the new set, and an empty replacement clears current holdings. `expected_snapshot` detects a newer save; same-date corrections create another snapshot rather than editing the old one.

These reported amounts and saved instrument metadata are not automatically refreshed from NAV. A snapshot is not a purchase ledger, proof of units or proof that every investment at an institution was supplied. The current-snapshot read is implemented; a public list/retrieve interface for every past snapshot is not implied by retaining old records.

## History supports only dates backed by evidence

A holding is scoped to a portfolio, investment account or folio, and asset. An exact dated observation can support that point with quantity still unknown. To reconstruct another date, the service needs an opening quantity, supported buy/sell transactions and a declared complete range covering the interval. A complete portfolio also requires a portfolio-wide declaration and support for every stored holding.

Completeness is asserted by the source or user, not independently certified. Observations and transaction replay describe the same position and are not added together. Conflicting evidence produces an unavailable result; the service does not invent balancing transactions. Transfers, splits and unsupported corporate actions cannot be treated as supported buys or sells.

## Positions and prices answer different questions

Keep the investor position date, valuation date and underlying fund disclosure cutoff separate. Existing historical mix valuation requires NAV on the exact valuation date. Monthly market snapshot selection can use an earlier observation, but that does not make a historical mix calculable when exact-date NAV is absent.

## Public interface to be agreed

Documentation proposal for review. This page describes the intended public resource organization, not a newly available endpoint. HTTP routes, SDK signatures and additional response fields still need agreement; no request is shown as executable.

A public current-valuation interface would need explicit position evidence, unit availability, actual NAV dates, freshness and missing-data outcomes. The existing saved-snapshot amount must not be labeled as a latest-NAV valuation. No external current-portfolio endpoint or SDK method is introduced here.

Scheme valuation accepts supplied units, but it does not prove ownership or establish an investor’s complete current portfolio. Private application operations remain outside this reference.

docs.title: Build with the Bharosa coding plugin
docs.content:
# Build with the Bharosa coding plugin

## What the plugin helps you build

Use Bharosa’s documentation tools to help your coding assistant find API methods, understand response fields and write an integration. You can connect without a Bharosa account. The tools read documentation and examples; they cannot read your portfolios or make API calls.

Start with the marketplace plugin below to install both the documentation tools and the `bharosa-integration` skill. The skill guides your assistant through planning, writing and testing an integration. Choose the hosted connection instead if you only need the documentation tools.

The tools use a versioned copy of the documentation rather than fetching the live website. The current hosted snapshot is 0.3.0 and targets SDK 0.4.0; its SDK 0.5.0 refresh is not yet published. For unified API keys and latest NAV, follow the current website and published bharosa@0.6.0 types rather than stale generated setup. The full plugin 0.3.0 release is available at https://github.com/bhafin/plugin/releases/tag/v0.3.0.

## Claude Code and Codex marketplace setup

The marketplace plugin adds the documentation server and the `bharosa-integration` skill together. The current GitHub marketplace plugin is version 0.3.0; the older standalone npm server described below remains version 0.2.1. Installing one does not update the other.

Use the commands for your chosen host, with Node and `npx` available on your PATH. Start a new host session after installation. Your host needs its own login, but you do not need a Bharosa account to read documentation.

## Connect to the hosted documentation service

Connect your coding assistant to https://mcp.bharosa.finance/ using Streamable HTTP. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is how the assistant discovers and calls these documentation tools. You do not need a Bharosa API key or authorization headers.

Before you start, install and sign in to either Codex CLI or Claude Code. Run only the command for your chosen host, then start a new session.

Codex CLI and Claude Code support this connection. Claude web setup at this address has not yet been verified. Public directory listings are pending, so use the direct connection instructions here.

After connecting, ask: “Use the Bharosa documentation to show me how to list an investor’s portfolios. Explain the setup, use the published TypeScript SDK, and add a test with fictional data.” Your assistant should find the relevant guide and examples before writing code.

## If the connection does not work

If Codex times out during startup, set `startup_timeout_sec = 30` in its `mcp_servers.bharosa_docs` configuration and restart the session.

If no tools appear, check the configured URL is https://mcp.bharosa.finance/ and restart your host. Opening that address in a browser is not a connection test: it accepts MCP requests. The health page at https://mcp.bharosa.finance/up can help you check whether the service is reachable.

If a search finds nothing, use a resource name such as portfolio or NAV, then read an example returned by the tool. Search matches words rather than interpreting every possible phrasing.

## Get help with the documentation tools

Report reproducible problems at https://github.com/bhafin/plugin/issues. Include the host, package or snapshot version, tool name and a synthetic example that shows the issue. These issues are public: do not post credentials, financial records or private queries. Remove sensitive details before sharing logs or screenshots.

## Find guides, methods and examples

Your assistant can browse with `bharosa_docs_list`, search with `bharosa_docs_search`, and open a result with `bharosa_docs_read`. Ask a concrete question, such as how to handle a stale portfolio edit.

For method details, `bharosa_api_search` finds an operation and `bharosa_api_details` explains its inputs, responses and errors. The assistant should use the returned operation ID rather than guess a route.

Use `bharosa_examples_search` and `bharosa_examples_read` to find TypeScript, shell or JSON examples. Keep the setup instructions with an example when adapting it. Sample data is for testing, not a real investor’s records.

All tool names start with `bharosa_`, so you can distinguish them from tools supplied by other plugins.

## Build and test a small integration

The marketplace plugin includes the `bharosa-integration` skill. It asks your assistant to understand the task, find the relevant API and examples, then write code and tests. Tell the assistant whether you are working with your own account or building an app for other users.

For example, ask: “Build a server-side portfolio list using Bharosa. Explain which IDs I need, show an empty state, and test an expired-token response with fictional data.” Review the generated code before using it. Keep keys and tokens in server configuration, never in chat or source code.

Start with fictional data so you can check empty results and errors without changing an account. Once those tests pass, follow the authentication guide to try a read-only request with authorized credentials.

## Run the server locally

For a local server, install a supported Node.js LTS version 22.12 or later. The older standalone npm package is `bharosa-docs-mcp@0.2.1`; its archived documentation does not cover the SDK 0.5.0 changes. You do not need API keys or a copy of the Bharosa website source.

Run the check command below before configuring your host. If it reports an error, resolve that error first. A successful check means the installed server can read its documentation; connecting it to your assistant is the next step.

## Connect the installed server to a stdio host

stdio means the host starts a process and exchanges protocol messages through standard input and output. For a host that supports this configuration shape, use the absolute supported Node executable and installed CLI paths below. This is an example, not a universal host configuration.

Use Node directly rather than npm start, whose banners can disrupt protocol output. A silent terminal process does not prove a connection. Verify that the host discovers all seven prefixed tools, then search and read a returned operation and example. The marketplace skill must be installed separately if you configure only the MCP server.

docs.content:
# Rehearse an integration

## Choose what you are demonstrating

For an offline demonstration, install bharosa@0.6.0 from npm and use its synthetic fixtures and the documentation MCP archive. Neither needs an account connection. Label sample investors, holdings and prices as fictional; installing a fixture package does not seed a running API or populate a real account.

For a service-backed demonstration, create an API key and enable only the own-account permissions needed for the demo. Use a consenting user’s grant for delegated private access. Check endpoint coverage and the actual response dates before presenting results. Do not put credentials into slides, source files or the MCP configuration.

## Run a small, observable sequence

First check that the SDK imports, then run a fictional-data example. If you use an AI assistant, ask it to find a method and read its example before generating code.

If service access is confirmed, begin with an account read and let the person select an authorized investor and portfolio. Display dates and unavailable values alongside results. Do not begin by saving demonstration holdings into an existing account. Any write rehearsal needs a specifically designated test account and authorization for that action.

Use the exact fund plan and option selected by the person. New supplied units allow at most four fractional digits; a rounded historical display is not a new observation. When showing a snapshot total, handle null as unavailable rather than zero.

## Keep an honest fallback

If credentials, connectivity or market coverage are missing, switch back to the explicitly labeled synthetic demonstration. Do not turn a cached response into a claim that a service call succeeded. For an uncertain write response, keep the original idempotency key and reconcile its outcome before trying a new operation.

Before presenting, check the flow at a narrow viewport, keyboard navigation, readable code examples and their copy buttons. Confirm links open the intended documentation version. Keep a short list of unverified steps, such as a desktop-host connection or deployed endpoint, rather than describing them as complete.

docs.content:
# Latest and monthly market data

## Before you integrate

Latest NAV and historical first-of-month market snapshots are available to every active API key without a separate approval or application registration. Use `bharosa.markets`; no account ID or investor token is needed. This is authenticated access, not anonymous access or permission to read anyone’s private portfolio.

Create one API key with market access included and optional own-account permissions left unchecked unless needed. Keep credentials server-only. Account-scoped methods still require their named permissions; delegated private access also requires user consent. All external historical market requests follow the same monthly date policy.

## Read latest and monthly NAV with one API key

Use a real scheme ID resolved through an authorized catalogue or supported mapping, not a fictional placeholder. For baseline discovery, see the SDK 0.6.0 market search in Build fund autocomplete; existing account catalogue search retains its permissions. Inspect status, observation_date and data before displaying a price. A missing snapshot has null data and observation_date.

Expense ratios, fund portfolios and fund holdings still require an explicit first-of-month asOf. Latest NAV does not enable arbitrary daily historical queries.

## A month start is a cutoff, not a price date

Request historical market snapshots for the first day of a month using asOf, such as 2026-08-01. The server selects the last eligible observation on or before that day. If the latest eligible price was observed on July 31, requested_date remains August 1 and observation_date remains July 31. No future observation is selected, and future requests are rejected using today in Asia/Kolkata.

A snapshot with status missing has null data and observation_date. This is different from an available expense observation whose stored value is null. Expense ratios are normalized by the data pipeline and returned unchanged: do not multiply or divide them by 100 based on an assumed provider format. Effective dates do not prove when information was publicly available.

For latest NAV, call `bharosa.markets.schemes.nav(schemeId)` without asOf. Read observation_date: latest does not mean a price was observed today. For an account-authorized current valuation, omit asOf in schemes.valuation and supply recorded units; read nav.date and freshness. You may retain latest observations over time, including daily; the monthly historical policy does not prevent that accumulation.

## Choose the right resource

Search mutualFunds for the investible scheme the user means, including its plan and option. Keep the returned scheme_id for NAV, expense and valuation calls. A fund owner is the fund whose underlying investments are disclosed; it is neither an investible scheme nor the AMC (fund house). Fund portfolio and holdings calls need that owner’s ID.

The external search example resolves scheme IDs, not a fund-owner catalogue. Obtain an owner ID through the supported data mapping in your environment before calling mutualFunds.portfolios.retrieve or mutualFunds.portfolios.holdings.list. Do not guess one from a scheme ID or copy a fictional number. A fund’s disclosed portfolio is also different from a person’s saved investment portfolio.

Holdings responses include the selected portfolio and a holdings page inside data. Keep the owner and asOf unchanged when passing holdings.next_cursor as startingAfter. Continue while has_more is true; a short page is not a completeness guarantee. This surface resolves the eligible disclosure itself and does not accept arbitrary historical portfolio IDs.

## Investor history keeps its actual dates

Monthly limits apply to historical market data for every external credential, including direct account keys. They do not restrict the dates on investor transactions, recorded positions or declared history ranges. Do not move an investor’s transaction to the first of the month to satisfy a market-data request.

Existing historical portfolio mix calculations still require exact-date NAV for valuation. They do not use the backward-as-of selection of marketSnapshots. A permitted first-of-month mix can therefore fail with historical_valuation_unavailable when no NAV exists on that exact date, including a non-trading first day. A monthly snapshot’s availability does not prove a historical mix is calculable.

Trusted internal access retains full market history through its separate interface. Neither policy supplies missing investor history, verifies ownership of user-supplied units, changes the allocation formulas, or grants data redistribution rights.

# Synthetic SDK samples

## Start with offline fixtures

The optional bharosa/testing export provides samplePortfolios and sampleFunds for deterministic UI tests. Importing it or calling these functions makes no network requests and needs no credentials. The main SDK entrypoint does not load these fixtures.

The scenarios use fictional synthetic: symbols and fixed January 1, 2026 dates. They are not real market instrument IDs, current prices or a calculation engine. Mapping a symbol to a real fund does not mean that fund has the fictional sample composition.

## Seeding is an explicit write

Use seedSamplePortfolio only with an authenticated account you control solely for development. Supply confirmTestAccount with the returned account ID, a stable runId, a scenario ID and an instruments mapping for every required synthetic symbol to an instrument resolved in that environment. The helper checks the account/mappings but cannot prove the account is a test environment. Never seed a customer or production account.

Nothing is seeded automatically. The helper creates reported dated snapshots, not invented transaction history or units; the empty scenario creates only an investor. Investor and portfolio creation are separate idempotent writes, not an atomic transaction. SampleSeedError.phase and investor identify the failed step and any known investor.

A lost response can follow a successful write. Retry with exactly the same account, runId, scenario and mapping; do not choose a new run ID to recover from a timeout. Changing the body under the same key can cause a conflict. Use a new run ID only when intentionally creating another sample.

docs.content:
# Finish your app’s sign-in setup

## What “Sign-in setup is not complete” means

Register your app in Developer settings with its name, website and exact callback URLs. Sign-in provisioning is asynchronous: check the displayed setup status and wait until the connection is ready before inviting users. Registration alone does not approve access to anyone’s private data.

Self-service app registration is available. Keep the existing registration while setup is pending rather than creating duplicates. If setup reports an error or is not ready, resolve that status before starting consent.

## What you can do now

In Developer settings, open your registered app and use Edit application details to check its name, website and callback URLs. A callback URL is the exact address in your app that receives the browser after the user finishes sign-in. It must point to a route your application actually handles; do not copy another app’s callback or use a guessed address.

Use HTTPS URLs. HTTP is allowed only for local development addresses such as localhost. URLs cannot contain embedded credentials, fragments beginning with #, or wildcard hosts. Register one to ten distinct callback URLs. Keep development and production settings separate.

Check the intended environment, exact callback URLs and account permissions your app needs. Do not paste secrets or user tokens into the name, website or callback fields. After changing registration details, check readiness again so the saved details and sign-in connection agree.

## Prepare your server integration

Once the app’s sign-in connection is ready, create its backend credential from the application setup. OAuth asks a user to authorize selected account data. Use the registered callback addresses and the permitted scopes—the named permissions your app may request.

The server integration must also securely identify the app, start the user’s authorization request and deliver resulting credentials to the correct server session. An application key belongs on your server; signing a user in does not by itself authorize access to their portfolio.

A backend credential identifies your application; it does not grant access to your own account or another person’s account. Private delegated requests also need the consenting user’s access token and the account authorized by that grant.

## Before you offer account connection to users

After setup reports ready, verify the connection in the intended environment: the app redirects to the registered callback, the user approves the intended account and permissions, and your server can make an authorized read. A saved registration is not evidence that those steps work.

Follow the app quickstart once you have the configured connection and credentials. The full market-history APIs remain restricted to Bharosa’s own apps. Latest NAV and monthly historical snapshots require no separate market-data approval. API authentication and account authorization still apply; finishing sign-in setup does not grant unrestricted history or permission to redistribute provider data.

Use a configured server-side client and the account permissions described in setup. List families, let the user choose one, then list its investors and select a person. Names are display labels, not unique IDs. Filter saved portfolios by the selected investor and let the user choose the portfolio.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.content:
# Introduction

## A clear model for investment data

Bharosa gives your application a consistent way to read and record investment data. You can organize a person’s portfolios, keep family members’ investments separate, and connect each position to a specific mutual fund instrument.

Start with an account: every request is checked against the account your credentials are allowed to access. Within that account, a Client groups people, an Investor represents one person, and a Portfolio groups that investor’s investment records. A Client here is a group such as a family; it is not the application you are building.

A portfolio’s name and owner are separate from its positions. A position describes the quantity or value of an instrument on a particular date. A holding gives that investment a continuing identity within a portfolio and investment account, so that observations and transactions can refer to it over time.

## Build with HTTP or TypeScript

Choose HTTP requests or the TypeScript SDK to call the same resource API from your server. The SDK supplies typed methods; it does not grant additional permissions or change the meaning of the data.

For a server integration accessing your own account, use a direct account key. If you are building an app for other users, use a delegated application key together with each user’s OAuth access token and account authorization. Signing in alone does not give an app access to portfolio data.

The quickstart offers setup paths for your own account and for an app serving other users. Both begin with a read-only account request. You will need an API key with the relevant own-account permissions, or the application credential and user grant for delegated access, before running it. All names, IDs and values in the examples are fictional; replace them with records returned by your configured service.

## India mutual funds, with context intact

The historical manual portfolio workflow supports India mutual funds with values entered in INR. Each save records a dated snapshot: a fixed set of positions and their reported values. A later save creates another snapshot rather than editing the old one.

Fund reference data helps you identify a scheme and display its net asset value (NAV), or value per unit, on a stated date. Refreshing a reference does not recalculate the values entered in a manual snapshot. A snapshot total is the sum of those entered values, not an investment return or a measure of all the investor’s wealth.

docs.content:
# Quickstart

## Start without credentials

You can build a small portfolio-list screen before connecting an account. First install the published SDK using the TypeScript SDK guide. You need Node.js 22.12 or later in a supported LTS release; no API key is needed for this first step.

Save the example below as `first-app.mjs` in the same folder where you installed bharosa, then run node `first-app.mjs`. The .mjs extension lets Node run the import directly; you do not need a TypeScript compiler for this example.

You should see four fictional portfolio summaries, including Synthetic new-investor with zero positions. Use that entry to design an empty state. These fixtures do not fetch current prices, calculate returns, seed an account or prove an API connection works.

## Connect a real account when you are ready

After the list and empty state work, create an API key in Developer settings. Market data access is included. Enable only the optional own-account permissions your integration needs. A successful website sign-in is not an API key, and installing the SDK does not create one.

If you cannot obtain the required key or app connection yet, continue with fictional data. Do not create placeholder secrets, copy another person’s account ID or keep retrying an unauthenticated request. The API-key and app-setup guides explain the prerequisites.

All active API keys include baseline market access. With `bharosa@0.6.0`, initialize `Bharosa` with your API key and use `bharosa.markets` for latest NAV and monthly NAVs, expense ratios, fund portfolios and fund holdings. No application registration, account ID or investor token is needed for these market calls. Private own-account operations require their optional permissions; another person’s account requires delegated consent. The legacy `BharosaMarket` client remains compatible.

## Choose your setup

Bharosa has one resource API and one TypeScript SDK. The setup differs according to whose account your code accesses. Once configured, both clients use the same methods to read accounts, investors and portfolios.

Before you start, store your API key in a server environment variable. The SDK uses the production API and defaults own-account selection to `me`; neither a base URL nor an account ID is required for this setup. Delegated requests use the account from the user’s grant. The examples report missing variables by name without exposing secrets.

## Work with your own account

For a script or server workload accessing an account you control, configure a direct account key. Start with a read-only account request before adding portfolio writes.

## Build an app for other users

For an app serving other people, use an application key with each user’s access token and authorized account. Register the application in Developer settings, wait for sign-in readiness and create its backend credential. Users must then authorize access to their account.

## Continue with the shared reference

After either setup, use the same resource methods. TypeScript reference snippets continue after the configured bharosa client. cURL examples include the credential headers for the selected setup.

docs.title: An app for other users
docs.content:
# An app for other users

## Implement the connection flow

Follow the complete connection guide for app-session creation, receipt exchange, token delivery, refresh and disconnect. These server calls use your application backend credential; never send it to browser JavaScript.

## Establish the connection integration first

Register your app in Developer settings and check its asynchronous setup status. Wait until its sign-in connection is ready, then create a backend credential and use the registered callback URLs for consent. Registration alone creates no user access grant. Before launch, verify the complete consent and authorized-read journey in your intended environment.

Before an external app can connect users, its registration, authenticated app sessions, consent initiation and secure token delivery need a trusted server integration. Do not substitute Bharosa’s browser sign-in routes or a user-entered account ID for that integration.

## What your server needs

This path is for an app accessing another person’s private account with permission. Register the app in Developer settings, check that its sign-in connection is ready and create a backend credential before starting consent. For your own account, use an API key with the required own-account permissions. Baseline market data uses any active API key without app registration, investor consent or an account ID.

A user access token is a short-lived credential representing one person’s permission for your app to access a specific account and scopes. Your server obtains it through the configured consent flow; it is not the app’s secret key, a password, or a sign-in ID token. Keep it server-side and handle expiry or revoked consent before requesting account data.

The first request below needs accounts:read. The application policy, key, token and active grant must all permit that scope. The application key alone gives no access to any account.

The TypeScript examples use the published `bharosa@0.6.0` npm package with Node.js 22.12 or later in a supported LTS release. Follow the SDK installation guide before running them. Keep keys, tokens and grant records on the server. Create a separate immutable client for each user grant.

## Configure a client for one authorized user

Keep your application key in server configuration. After the user completes consent, your server’s validated callback exchanges the authorization response and stores the resulting access token and account ID in that user’s server session. Load that stored grant for each request; do not ask the user to find or paste a token.

The response contains the account authorized by that grant. Both onboarding paths now use the same resource methods: the invocation below is identical to the own-account request.

## Make the same request over HTTP

This HTTP alternative is for server-side diagnostics after your configured callback has obtained the grant; the user does not type these tokens. Populate the account ID and access-token variables from that same stored grant. Send both headers. Authorization identifies the application key; Bharosa-User-Authorization carries the user’s access token. Use the account selected in that grant. A successful request returns 200 OK and the account object.

## Resolve access failures before continuing

For 401, check both credentials and token expiry. Refresh only through the validated server lifecycle when a refresh token was issued; revoked or invalid grants require fresh authorization. Do not retry unchanged credentials indefinitely.

For 403, check the grant’s account and the permissions shared by the application policy, key and token. Additional scopes need explicit authorization. Once the read succeeds, continue with the shared reference or first-portfolio walkthrough; fund lookup also requires an available authorized market-data provider.

docs.content:
# Your own account

## Before you begin

This walkthrough reads your account and investors without changing data. Create an API key with the optional accounts:read and investors:read own-account permissions. Market access is included but does not grant these private reads. The SDK selects your own account as `me`.

For the portfolio workflow that follows, also obtain clients:read and portfolios:read. Saving a portfolio requires portfolios:write. Fund lookup requires an available, authorized market-data provider. Documentation access does not itself provision an API account or activate that provider.

Store `BHAROSA_SECRET_KEY` in your server environment. The fictional key shown elsewhere in these docs will not authenticate.

The SDK examples use the published `bharosa@0.6.0` npm package and Node.js 22.12 or later in a supported LTS release. Follow the SDK installation guide before running them. You can also use the HTTP example below. For an app serving other users, complete the OAuth setup first instead of substituting their account ID into this direct-key example.

## Initialize your server client

Create a client on your server with your API key. The two calls below retrieve the account and the first ten investor profiles. Keep the key out of browser bundles, mobile apps, source control, URLs and logs.

On success, account contains the authorized account’s details, while investors.data contains the profiles you can select for a portfolio. Keep the IDs returned by the API; the example IDs in this documentation do not identify your records.

## Make the same request over HTTP

If you prefer HTTP, this cURL command makes the same account retrieval request. It should return 200 OK with an account object. All resource paths start with /v1; changing the account in the path does not change what your key is allowed to access.

If you receive 401, check that the key is present, valid and unexpired. A 403 response means the credentials do not authorize the requested operation or account. Resolve those conditions before adding write operations to your integration.

## Save your first holdings

Once the read requests succeed, choose an investor from investors.data and follow the first-portfolio guide. You will search for a fund instrument, submit an entered current value, and receive a snapshot containing the saved positions and their total.

Keep the returned `snapshot.id` when you open an editor. The next save uses that ID to detect whether someone else has updated the portfolio in the meantime.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.content:
# Authentication

## Authentication versus authorization

Choose credentials according to whose account your code will access. “Your own account” examples use a direct account key: a secret assigned to a server workload you control, with access to one account. Send it in Authorization: Bearer <secret API key>.

Each key has named permissions called scopes. For example, portfolios:read permits reading portfolio data, while portfolios:write is needed to save it. The API checks both the account and the operation’s required scope. Replacing an account ID in the URL never expands a key’s access.

## Acting for a user

Choose “An app for other users” when a registered application needs to access accounts on its users’ behalf. This is delegated access. The application has its own key, and each user separately authorizes access to a selected account through OAuth.

Send the application key in Authorization: Bearer <key> and the user’s access token in Bharosa-User-Authorization: Bearer <access token>. Both credentials must belong to the same registered application, and the selected account must match the active user grant. The application key alone grants no account access, even to the application owner’s account.

The API allows only permissions shared by the key, token, active grant and application policy. Do not pair a direct account key with a user token. Invalid supplied credentials are rejected rather than silently treated as another authentication mode.

OpenID Connect sign-in identifies a user. OAuth consent authorizes data access. An ID token from sign-in is not an API access token, and signing in does not by itself authorize your application to read a portfolio.

## Respond to access failures

401 means authentication is missing, expired or invalid. Reauthenticate or replace the invalid credential; do not loop requests unchanged. 403 means the authenticated caller lacks permission: request the specific scope or account consent.

404 resource_missing is used for missing or foreign-account resources. Do not probe other account IDs or infer existence from authorization failures.

docs.title: API keys
docs.content:
# API keys

## Choose the smallest useful scope

Read scopes are accounts:read, clients:read, investors:read and portfolios:read. Mutation scopes are investors:write and portfolios:write. Account-scoped fund search and references use portfolios:read; the separate baseline market search does not.

Use Create API key for one key with market data access included. Optional own-account permissions start unchecked; enable only those your workload needs. App registration is not required for market-only access. A delegated application backend credential is created separately in application setup and grants no direct access to the owner’s or anyone else’s private account. Separate credentials by workload and environment. A family profile is data, not permission to act as that family member.

## Store and use keys safely

Inject secrets through your server environment or secret store. Do not use browser-exposed environment-variable prefixes. Redact authorization headers, cookies and tokens from request logs.

In signed-in Developer settings, choose Create API key, optional own-account permissions and expiry. A new secret is shown once. If creation or rotation has an uncertain outcome, refresh the key list before another change. A lost secret cannot be recovered; reconcile the listed key, revoke it and create a replacement rather than retrying blindly.

The literal bh_sk_FICTIONAL_DO_NOT_USE is only a documentation placeholder. Do not embed it as a working fallback.

## Rotate and revoke

Rotation creates a replacement while both keys remain active until expiry or explicit revocation. Update dependent deployments, verify access using an operation permitted by the key’s scopes, then explicitly revoke the old key. Rotation alone does not secure a compromised key.

If a key is exposed, revoke it promptly, replace it, and review access. Revocation removes application-key access; OAuth grant revocation independently removes delegated user access. Never store credentials in idempotency keys.

docs.title: OAuth & user authorization
docs.content:
# OAuth & user authorization

## A consent-based authorization flow

Use a confidential server application or a browser application backed by your server. An app running entirely in a browser or on a user’s device cannot keep an application secret; direct browser/mobile token handling requires a separately registered public-client integration. Account-key and delegated SDK configuration is server-only.

Register the application in Developer settings and check the asynchronous setup status. A pending or `setup_required` status is not readiness to connect users. When the connection is ready, create its backend credential and use its exact registered redirect URI, required scopes and configured authorization and token endpoints. Initiate the authorization-code flow with state and PKCE; retain the verifier on the initiating session.

The user signs in and chooses the account and requested permissions to grant. On callback, validate state, exchange the code with the original redirect URI and verifier, and bind the returned grant to that user session. Reject callbacks that do not match an initiated transaction.

Bharosa’s /auth/login and /auth/callback routes belong to its browser sign-in flow. They are not portfolio resource endpoints or substitutes for an application’s registered redirect URI.

## Send delegated context from your server

Keep tokens server-side. Initialize the SDK with auth.type delegated_application, its apiKey and userAccessToken; account must be the grant’s account ID. Do not trust an account ID supplied by the browser as authorization.

The access token authorizes data access; an ID token identifies a signed-in user and must not be sent as a data API access token.

## Expiry, consent and revocation

Respect token expiry and granted scopes. Use a refresh token only when one was issued and store any rotated replacement atomically. On `invalid_grant` or revoked consent, stop delegated requests and ask the user to reconnect.

In the production app, signing out clears your Bharosa browser session and opens Auth0 logout. It does not sign you out of Google or disconnect an application. To stop an app accessing an account, disconnect that app: Bharosa access stops immediately, while revocation at the sign-in provider may finish later.

Developer settings distinguishes Connected, Delivery pending, Reconnect required, Revoked and Provider revocation pending. Provider revocation pending means local access is already revoked. Retry provider revocation explicitly retries upstream cleanup without restoring local access; refreshing the list alone does not retry it. Reconnect requires fresh approval. A new browser login requires reconnect for that browser-bound integration.

Refresh connection recovers an existing pending server delivery before requesting another refresh. Tokens stay server-side. An uncertain provider exchange requires fresh consent; do not replay its callback or treat sign-in as approval.

Do not broaden permissions silently. Additional scopes or a different account require explicit authorization. Disconnecting an application revokes its grant; retaining a secret application key does not preserve delegated access.

docs.title: Accounts & resources
docs.content:
# Accounts & resources

## Resource definitions

An Account is the access boundary for the records in these docs. Its id identifies the account, and primary_investor may identify a profile or be null. The public response does not expose the internal owner user ID. Its optional name is a display label and can differ from the owner’s name.

personal_client_id is the authenticated person’s household group in this account. Machine account keys return null; a missing personal link also returns null. The schema permits omission, which provides no context. This is not a membership grant or a user directory. accounts.retrieve() uses your configured account, so no repeated account ID is needed. If there is no personal client, let the caller select an authorized client rather than guessing from a name or primary investor.

A Client groups investors within an account, for example under “My family.” Its account field links it to that account. This use of Client is unrelated to an OAuth application or SDK client, and creating a family profile does not grant anyone login access.

An Investor represents a person. Its client and account fields identify where the profile belongs. relationship_to_owner is self, spouse, child, parent, sibling or other. Use the investor ID for requests because two people can have the same name.

A Portfolio belongs to an investor and stores metadata such as name and reporting_currency. Retrieve its current snapshot separately to obtain positions and values. That separation lets you read a portfolio’s identity without assuming its current holdings are embedded in the metadata response.

## Opaque IDs and ownership

Normal resource IDs use a type prefix and 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters: acct_, clt_, inv_, ptf_, iac_, psn_ and pos_. Treat all identifiers as opaque; instrument identifiers can be catalogue-specific.

The account alias me resolves the authorized account context. It is not a way to enumerate another user’s accounts. Client filters organize records within existing permission boundaries.

## Representing a family

One self investor represents the owner. Create additional profiles in the same family Client and save each portfolio with its investor ID. Adding an investor does not invite them or create shared login access.

A Client association is fixed on investor creation. Select the family explicitly when there is more than one Client; never infer it from the first list result or a matching name.

docs.title: Portfolios & snapshots
docs.content:
# Portfolios & snapshots

## The snapshot response

A portfolio groups an investor’s investments. Its investment account is the container in which holdings are recorded; in history workflows this can distinguish separate folios. A holding identifies one asset within that portfolio and investment account. A position describes what was observed or reconstructed for the holding on a date.

For manual portfolios, a snapshot records the complete set of entered positions at one effective date. The response includes portfolio and investment_account metadata, the snapshot revision, and positions. investment_account.latest_snapshot points to the currently selected revision.

Each position links an instrument to the snapshot. Amount-based entries contain a reported INR valuation and unknown quantity. A units-first entry stores a positive quantity with null valuation; it does not invent an amount. cost_basis remains null. The instruments collection preserves the reference metadata attached when the snapshot was saved.

Read `total_current_value` for the exact sum of entered values and `snapshot.as_of` for their effective date. Amount-only snapshots use manual_current_value. If any position contains only supplied units, the total is null and valuation_basis is supplied_quantity: unavailable is not zero. The separate market_data field describes reference data; it does not turn an entered value into a calculated return.

## Interpret missing values correctly

Null quantity and cost mean unknown, not zero. A current value does not imply units, purchase price, profit or tax cost. Do not divide by NAV to fabricate quantity.

created is ingestion time in Unix seconds. as_of is the financial date with Asia/Kolkata context. Reference NAV has its own date, which may differ from the holdings date.

## A complete set on every save

`current_snapshot` selects the latest revision and is mutable. Each returned snapshot and its pinned instrument metadata are immutable. Snapshot IDs are revision tokens; this interface does not expose history retrieval by ID.

A replacement publishes all supported positions in one snapshot. Omit a fund to remove it. Send positions: [] to clear holdings. Previous snapshots remain immutable.

Use expected_snapshot to prevent a stale editor overwriting a newer save. Same-date corrections are allowed; older effective dates cannot replace newer holdings.

docs.title: Decimal money & dates
docs.content:
# Decimal money & dates

## Decimal strings, not floating-point numbers

Send current_value as a nonnegative plain decimal string, with at most 20 integer digits and 18 fractional digits. Examples: "0", "125000.50", "2456.789". Do not send numbers, commas, exponents, NaN or negative values.

Amounts are in INR major units. The canonical response may remove trailing zeroes, so "125000.50" and "125000.5" have the same value. Use a decimal library for arithmetic and formatting; do not round before submission. Totals can exceed a single position’s bound.

## Keep financial dates explicit

Use a real YYYY-MM-DD calendar date in Asia/Kolkata, from 1900-01-01 through today. Same-date corrections create a new snapshot; a replacement cannot move the effective date backward.

An as_of object with precision date retains date and time_zone. Do not convert a date-only observation into an invented UTC instant. created is a Unix-second ingestion timestamp, not financial freshness.

docs.title: Pagination
docs.content:
# Pagination

## Request the next page

Client, investor and portfolio lists return a page at a time. Omit `starting_after` for the first request and choose limit from 1 to 100; the default is 10. The response’s data array contains that page’s records.

If `has_more` is true, request the next page using the last data item’s ID as `starting_after` and keep the same filters. The SDK spells this option startingAfter. Stop when `has_more` is false. The returned url is the resource path, not a saved copy of your query filters.

Fund search and exact reference lookup have their own result limits and do not use these cursors. Multiple list requests are not a frozen view: records can change while you are moving through pages.

## Ordering and recovery

In the reviewed local SDK, malformed resource pages throw `InvalidResponseError`: duplicate IDs within a page, an empty page claiming more results, the incoming exclusive cursor appearing again, or more records than requested. Do not treat that failure as an empty successful list. Your multi-page loop should also track seen IDs and cursors, stop on overlap or cycles, and show a recoverable error rather than silently dropping records.

Lists are newest first, with descending ID as the tie-breaker. Cursor ordering uses full stored creation precision even when created is returned in seconds.

A missing, foreign-account or out-of-filter cursor returns 400 invalid_cursor. Restart with the intended filters and deduplicate by ID if records changed during traversal. A multi-page walk is not a frozen account-wide snapshot.

docs.title: Idempotency
docs.content:
# Idempotency

## One key per logical operation

Send Idempotency-Key for investor creation, portfolio creation and snapshot replacement. Investor updates also accept a key; use one whenever the request might be retried. An investor profile update is a partial update with last-write-wins fields; snapshot updates instead require expected_snapshot. Generate a unique key per new operation, for example with crypto.randomUUID().

Reuse the same key only with the same account, method, route and JSON body after a timeout or retryable failure. Object key ordering is ignored; array ordering and decimal-string spelling are significant. A changed body under the same key returns a conflict. Never use a person’s name, credentials or account data as the key.

## Understand the replay window

Successful responses are retained for 24 hours from when the server records the successful response. The record and mutation commit atomically; retries do not extend retention. Every retry rechecks current credential, account, scope and grant authorization before replay. An authorized identical retry returns the original result, even if a newer snapshot now exists; it does not refresh NAV.

After that window, reconcile current resources before resubmitting an uncertain write. A new key can create a new operation. Validation and conflict errors need corrective action, not blind repetition.

docs.title: Errors & recovery
docs.content:
# Errors & recovery

## When the example fails before an API request

If Node cannot find the bharosa package, run the example from the project where you installed it and confirm `npm list bharosa` reports version 0.6.0. Do not run SDK contributor commands from an installed package; follow the installation guide’s commands instead.

If an import reports that `BharosaMarket` is not exported, check the example’s version requirement. That compatibility client is exported by `bharosa@0.6.0`; new integrations can use `Bharosa` and its `markets` namespace. Check `npm list bharosa` and update an older installation before retrying; changing credentials cannot fix an import error.

A `Missing BHAROSA_…` configuration error comes from the setup example before it sends a request. Add the named value to your server environment and restart the process. Check that the variable is present without printing its secret value.

## The error envelope

When a request fails, read the error object before deciding whether to retry. type is the broad category, code identifies the condition, and message explains it. param points to the relevant input when one is available.

Keep request_id and the HTTP status in diagnostic logs so you can trace a failed request. Leave credentials and personal request bodies out of those logs. The example below shows a save rejected because the snapshot changed while an editor was open.

## Choose the right recovery

A 400 response usually needs a corrected request. For invalid_cursor, restart the list with the intended filters. For invalid_instruments, check the exact instrument IDs and remove duplicates. Repeating the same invalid request will not fix it.

For 401, replace missing, expired or invalid credentials. For 403, obtain the required scope or account authorization. A 404 resource_missing means the record is missing or is not accessible in the selected account; verify the account and ID instead of probing other accounts.

A 409 response needs attention to the specific conflict. For snapshot_conflict, fetch the current snapshot and reconcile it with the user’s draft. For self_investor_exists, retrieve the existing self profile. For an idempotency conflict, compare the body with the original request; use a new key only if you intend a new operation.

If a history import times out, keep the original body and idempotency key. The save may already have completed even if your client did not receive its response. Reconcile or retry that same operation before starting another import; cancelling a request does not guarantee that nothing was saved.

For 429, honor Retry-After when present. For a network timeout or transient 502, 503 or 504, retry a limited number of times with increasing, randomized delays. Preserve the original body and idempotency key for writes. A timeout means the outcome is unknown, not necessarily that the save failed.

If market_data_unavailable is returned with 503, keep the saved holdings visible and retry the reference lookup later. An unavailable reference must not become an invented price or erase the user’s data.

## Keep retries bounded

409 request_in_progress means another attempt with the same key is still running; retry that unchanged request within your retry budget. Do not automatically retry other conflicts or all 4xx responses. Cap transient retries and show a recoverable failure state. Never replace a failed reference lookup with invented prices or hide saved holdings because the market provider is unavailable.

docs.title: Build your first portfolio
docs.content:
# Build your first portfolio

## 1. Select the investor and fund

Begin with the configured server client from either onboarding path. Retrieve the account, list its investors, and select the person whose portfolio you want to create. Use that persisted investor ID rather than a name or a fictional ID from an example.

Next, search mutual funds using at least two characters and let the user choose a resolved instrument. Show the scheme, plan and option together. Fund lookup and saving need available, authorized market-reference data; if lookup returns 503, retain the draft and retry later instead of guessing an instrument ID.

## 2. Submit the initial positions

The request below illustrates a portfolio with its initial positions. Replace the fictional investor and instrument IDs with your selections. Supply a portfolio name, an effective date in the India calendar, and a `positions` array containing up to 100 distinct instruments. Use an empty array to create a portfolio before adding holdings. For an amount-based position, send `current_value` as an INR decimal string. Each position may instead supply a positive quantity decimal string with at most four fractional digits, never both quantity and current_value. The same as_of date records when the units were observed. A NAV is not required to save them. Snapshot replacement still requires amounts.

Generate one idempotency key for this intended save. It identifies the operation if a connection fails and you need to retry. Keep that key and the unchanged request body until you know the outcome; a new key represents a new operation.

## Create from units you already know

After choosing the investor and exact fund instrument, record a positive unit count with at most four fractional digits and its observation date. Five fractional digits are rejected even if the last digit is zero; input is not silently rounded. These are fictional placeholders: replace both IDs with the records selected above. Do not infer units from a guessed price or supply an invented amount.

The save does not need a NAV. In its snapshot response, `quantity` contains the supplied units and `valuation` is null. If any position has no reported amount, `total_current_value` is null and `valuation_basis` is `supplied_quantity`. Display an unavailable value rather than zero. This does not calculate a current NAV valuation or change snapshot-replacement inputs.

## 3. Display the result

A successful creation returns 201 Created with the portfolio and its first snapshot. Display result.positions and `total_current_value` together with `snapshot.as_of`, so the user can see the date the entered values describe. Handle a null total explicitly when units-only positions are present.

Keep `snapshot.id` for the next edit. When the page reloads, retrieve `current_snapshot` to recover the saved positions; retrieving portfolio metadata alone will not return them. If you also show a reference NAV, label it with its own date and freshness instead of using it to silently replace the entered values.
